title: Steel Is Designed Twice, and Decided in the Connections
summary: A steel frame is designed by the engineer of record and then redesigned piece by piece on the fabricator's shop drawings. Connections carry the load path and need a clear owner and real margin. A half-built frame needs its own stability plan.
body:
A steel frame is designed twice: once by the engineer of record on the contract drawings, and again by the fabricator on the shop drawings. The building stands or falls on the second design, and most of that second design lives in the connections.

Recall

Q. Who designs formwork and reshoring, and why does that boundary matter?

A. Formwork and reshoring are usually temporary works designed by the contractor's own engineer, while the engineer of record states what the permanent structure can carry at each age. If nobody owns the boundary, a young slab can end up carrying loads that nobody checked.

Q. Why does the water-cement ratio matter so much for durability?

A. A lower ratio leaves less pore space in the hardened paste, so the concrete is stronger and less permeable. Less permeability means water and chlorides reach the reinforcing steel more slowly, which delays corrosion.

Q. Why does a taller building need booster pumps or break tanks?

A. Street pressure can only lift water so far. Booster pumps raise pressure for the upper floors, and storage tanks buffer demand and protect the public supply from backflow.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, as owner you will never weld a beam, but you will approve the schedule, pay the fabricator, and live with the frame for fifty years. Structural steel and factory-built components move more of the building's risk off site and earlier in time. Decisions you never see, made at a drafting desk in a fabrication shop months before erection, decide whether the frame is safe, whether it fits, and whether it arrives on time. This week Bram teaches you where those decisions sit, so you can ask the right questions of the right people.

The load path runs through the connections

In plain English: a beam is only as strong as the bolts and welds that hold it to the column. A strong member with a weak connection is a weak structure.

The professional framing is the load path: the continuous route by which every load travels from where it is applied, through slabs, beams, connections, columns and foundations, down into the ground. Members are easy to see on a drawing. Connections are where force changes direction, concentrates and transfers, and they are where steel structures most often fail. American practice for structural steel runs on the American Institute of Steel Construction specification, known as AISC 360, for design, and the AISC Code of Standard Practice, known as AISC 303, for how responsibility is shared between owner, engineer, fabricator and erector. Welding follows the American Welding Society structural code, AWS D1.1, and high-strength bolting follows the Research Council on Structural Connections specification. Verify the editions against the current adopted edition before you rely on any of them.

A new term: delegated connection design. On many projects the engineer of record designs the members and gives the forces each connection must carry, then delegates the detailed connection design to a licensed engineer working for the fabricator. The Code of Standard Practice recognises more than one way to divide that work [unverified — confirm independently]. The contract must say which one applies, who stamps the calculations, and who reviews them. When the contract is silent, the gap becomes an argument after something goes wrong.

A worked example, with hypothetical round numbers. A floor beam carries a factored end reaction of 200 kilonewtons. The engineer of record shows that number on the drawings. The fabricator's engineer designs a shear connection with a row of bolts and a plate welded to the column. Each bolt in single shear has a hypothetical design strength of 50 kilonewtons, so four bolts give 200 kilonewtons, exactly the demand. Bram would reject that design on instinct, not because the arithmetic is wrong, but because there is no margin for the plate, the weld, the bolt bearing on thin material, or a reaction that grows when the architect moves a partition. A fifth bolt costs almost nothing in the shop and a great deal once the beam is in the air.

Say that out loud now.

Shop drawings: the second design

In plain English: the fabricator redraws your building piece by piece, and those drawings, not the architect's, are what the shop actually cuts and welds.

A shop drawing is a fabricator's detailed drawing of each piece and connection, showing dimensions, holes, welds, bolts and marks for erection. Shop drawings are submittals. They go to the engineer of record for review, usually through the architect and the contractor. The review stamp matters. A stamp reading reviewed or no exceptions taken means the engineer found the submittal in general conformance with the design intent. It does not usually make the engineer the guarantor of every dimension, and it does not relieve the fabricator of its own duty to get the piece right. Read your design contract to see exactly what review your engineer has promised.

A second worked example, hypothetical. The frame has 800 pieces released in four sequences of 200. The engineer's contract allows 10 working days to review each submittal. The fabricator needs approved drawings 6 weeks before it can ship a sequence, and the erector needs the first sequence on site in week 20. Work backward: the first approved package is needed by week 14, so its review starts by week 12, so the fabricator must submit in week 12 at the latest, which means detailing starts around week 6. If the engineer returns the first package marked revise and resubmit, one more review cycle of 2 weeks pushes erection to week 22 unless the fabricator absorbs it. The shop drawing schedule is a critical path item, not paperwork.

The frame is weakest when it is half built

In plain English: a finished steel frame is braced by its floors and walls. A half-built one is not, and it can fall over in a storm while every piece is perfectly made.

Erection stability is the strength and stiffness of the partly built frame against wind, construction loads and accidental impact, before the permanent bracing, floor diaphragms and connections are all complete. It is usually the erector's responsibility, achieved with temporary bracing, guy cables and a planned erection sequence. Federal safety rules for steel erection sit in OSHA 1926 Subpart R, which covers matters such as anchor bolts, column stability during erection and fall protection; verify the current text before you rely on it.

Prefabrication pushes the same problem earlier. A volumetric module, a bathroom pod or a precast panel is a finished piece of building made in a factory, then trucked, lifted and set. That makes two new questions: who checks quality inside a factory you cannot walk every day, and who owns the piece once you have paid for it but before it leaves the yard. Both return later this week.

How the best do it

The strongest building contractors treat steel as a manufacturing schedule, not a site activity. They hold a connection design meeting before detailing starts, lock the connection types the fabricator prefers, freeze the column grid and floor elevations early, and track every submittal on a dated register reviewed weekly. A small developer can copy all of that: require a connection design kickoff, a submittal register and a written erection plan before the steel contract is signed.

Six-Lens Check

Tax: payments to an off-site fabricator may raise questions about when costs are capitalised and where goods are supplied; verify that against the primary source before you rely on it. Liability: the contract must state who designs connections and temporary bracing, or the gap is yours. Banking: lenders often refuse to fund materials not yet on site unless title and insurance are proven. Governance: approval of connection changes belongs in the owner's decision log, not a phone call. Estate: none directly, except that personal guarantees on a delayed frame belong in your estate records. Exit: a buyer's engineer will ask for the stamped shop drawings and connection calculations, so archive them.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is a connection change made late, for convenience, and approved without anyone recalculating the load path. The control is a rule written into the steel contract: any change to a connection detail after first review goes back to the engineer of record with calculations, and nothing is fabricated from it until that review is returned.

The beginner's mistake

Treating the engineer's review stamp as a guarantee and the shop drawings as clerical work. The stamp is a limited review, and the shop drawings are the real design of every piece that will be cut.

Callback

In Week 52, Marco taught delivery methods and buyout, and Week 49 taught that exclusions in a scope are where money leaks. Steel is the sharpest example: connection design, temporary bracing, shop drawing review time and stored-material insurance are the four items most often missing from a steel scope, and each becomes a change order if left out.

Recap

Steel is designed twice, and the fabricator's shop drawings are the design that gets built. The load path runs through connections, which need margin and a clear owner. Shop drawing review is on the critical path. A half-built frame needs its own stability plan, and prefabrication moves quality and title questions off site.

Next: Ford on Failure Forensics: a hanging walkway, one changed connection and a collapse that reshaped engineering responsibility.
checklist: The steel contract states who designs the connections and who stamps the calculations.
I have a dated submittal register with review periods agreed in writing.
The shop drawing schedule is on the critical path, worked backward from the first erection date.
Any connection change after first review goes back to the engineer of record with calculations.
The erector has a written erection and temporary bracing plan before steel arrives.
I know what my engineer's review stamp does and does not promise.
Stamped shop drawings and connection calculations are archived for the life of the building.
Title and insurance for off-site steel are settled before I pay for it.
head: Field checklist
speak: A steel frame is designed twice. The engineer of record designs the members and states the forces. The fabricator then redraws every piece on shop drawings, and those drawings are what the shop actually cuts and welds. The building's strength runs along the load path, and the load path runs through the connections, where force changes direction and concentrates. So I want three things settled in the contract: who designs the connections, who stamps the calculations, and how long review takes. Shop drawing review sits on the critical path, so I schedule it backward from the first erection date. A half-built frame is at its weakest, so the erector needs a written stability and bracing plan. And any connection change after review goes back to the engineer with calculations before anything is fabricated. Prefabrication moves the same quality and ownership questions into a factory, which I will deal with before I pay for anything off site.
terms: Shop drawing — a fabricator's detailed drawing of each piece and connection, used to cut, drill, weld and erect it.
Delegated connection design — an arrangement in which the engineer of record gives connection forces and a licensed engineer for the fabricator designs the connections.
Erection stability — the ability of a partly built frame to resist wind, construction loads and impact before permanent bracing and floors are complete.

hostile.q: Your fabricator wants to change a connection to speed up erection. Your engineer says it looks fine. Why are you holding it up?
hostile.a: Looks fine is not a review. A connection change alters the load path, and the rule in our contract is that it goes back to the engineer of record with calculations before anything is fabricated. If the change is sound, that costs a few days. If it is not, it is the difference between a delay and a failure. I will press the engineer for a fast turnaround, but I will not skip the calculation.

title: The Hyatt Regency Walkways: One Changed Connection
summary: In 1981 two suspended walkways at the Hyatt Regency in Kansas City collapsed, killing 114 people. A hanger rod detail was changed on the shop drawings for convenience, the change doubled the load on a connection that was already too weak, and the review did not recalculate it. The case is about owning every change to a load path.
body:
On 17 July 1981, two suspended walkways fell into the crowded atrium of the Hyatt Regency hotel in Kansas City, Missouri, and 114 people died. The cause was one connection detail, changed between design and fabrication, that nobody recalculated.

Recall

Q. What is delegated connection design?

A. An arrangement in which the engineer of record gives the forces each connection must carry and a licensed engineer working for the fabricator designs the connection itself. The contract must say who stamps and who reviews.

Q. What is a low break in concrete testing?

A. A cylinder or core result below the specified strength. It triggers investigation, often coring and engineering review, rather than automatic demolition.

Q. What are the main ASCE 7 load categories an engineer combines?

A. Dead load, live load, wind, snow where relevant, earthquake and others such as flood, each multiplied by factors in defined combinations. Verify the current edition before you rely on specifics.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, this is the case structural engineers are taught first, and it is about the exact boundary Bram drew yesterday: the line between the engineer's design and the fabricator's shop drawings. The building was new. The steel was not defective. A detail was changed for convenience, a review did not catch what the change did to the load path, and the walkways came down under a crowd at a tea dance. Ford takes it through seven steps.

1. Timeline

The hotel was designed in the late 1970s with an atrium crossed by walkways at the second, third and fourth levels. The fourth-level walkway hung directly above the second-level walkway, both supported from the roof framing by hanger rods. The original design showed each hanger as a single continuous rod running from the roof, through the fourth-level walkway's box beam, and down to the second-level box beam, with nuts holding each beam on the rod. During shop drawing preparation the detail was changed to two separate rods: one from the roof to the fourth-level beam, and a second from the fourth-level beam down to the second-level beam. The hotel opened in 1980. On the evening of 17 July 1981, with people standing on the walkways and filling the atrium floor, the fourth-level box beam connections failed and both walkways fell.

2. Key decisions

The decisive decision was the change from one rod to two. A continuous rod is awkward to build: it has to be threaded along most of its length, and a nut must be run a long way up it to reach the upper walkway. Two shorter rods are easier. The second decision was the review. The changed detail appeared on the shop drawings, those drawings went through the engineer's office, and they came back approved without the change being recalculated.

3. Assumptions

The working assumption was that the change was a fabrication convenience, not a structural one. It looks like a minor detail on a sheet. It is not. With the continuous rod, the fourth-level beam carried only its own walkway; the lower walkway's load passed down the rod and up to the roof without bearing on the upper beam's nut. With two rods, the lower walkway hung from the upper beam, so the upper beam's connection now carried both walkways. The load on that critical connection roughly doubled. Investigators also found that the original detail was itself weaker than the building code required, so the change took an already marginal connection well past failure.

Say that out loud now.

4. Incentives

Every party faced pressure to keep the project moving. A fabricator is rewarded for buildable, fast details. An engineering office reviewing hundreds of shop drawing sheets is rewarded for turning them around on time. Nobody was rewarded for stopping and asking what a small change did to the force flow. That is not a story about bad people. It is a story about a system in which the incentive to finish beat the incentive to check.

5. Warning signs ignored

Reports from the investigation and the later licensing proceedings describe warning signs during construction, including a partial collapse of part of the atrium roof during construction that prompted a review of the structure. The connections that failed were not identified at that time. A review prompted by one failure that does not trace every load path is a warning sign in itself. A detail that changes how loads are shared between two members should always be a warning sign on a shop drawing.

6. Point of no return

The point of no return was the approval of the shop drawings with the two-rod detail. After that, the steel was fabricated, erected and covered, and the defect sat hidden inside finished box beams. No routine inspection after occupancy would have found it. Once the pieces were made to the changed drawing, only a deliberate structural recheck could have saved the walkways.

7. Root cause

The root cause was a gap in responsibility for connection design. Each party could believe someone else had checked the change. In the licensing proceedings that followed, the engineers of record lost their professional licences in Missouri, and the case is widely taught as establishing that the engineer of record carries responsibility for the structural integrity of the design, including changes that arrive through shop drawings. The technical cause was a doubled load on a connection that was already too weak. The organisational cause was that no single person owned the question of whether the change was safe.

A worked example of the force flow

Use hypothetical round numbers to see the doubling. Say each walkway puts a load of 100 kilonewtons on one hanger point. With one continuous rod, the nut under the fourth-level beam carries that beam's 100 kilonewtons, and the nut under the second-level beam carries the lower 100 kilonewtons, which travels up the rod past the upper beam. With two rods, the upper beam's connection carries its own 100 kilonewtons plus the 100 kilonewtons hanging from it below: 200 kilonewtons on the same nut and the same thin box beam section. Nothing on the drawing grew. The demand on one point doubled.

A second example, the owner's version. A hypothetical project issues 600 shop drawing sheets in four months. The engineer's office logs 40 changes from the contract design, most of them dimensional. If the review procedure requires the reviewer to flag any change that alters how load is shared between members, and to attach a calculation before approval, the office reviews perhaps three or four of the 40 in depth. That is a small cost against the risk.

What changed afterward

The profession drew a clear lesson. Contracts and codes of practice now spell out far more explicitly who designs connections, who stamps the calculations and what a shop drawing review covers, and many engineering offices treat review of any structural change as design work rather than checking. For an owner, the practical copy is simple: make the responsibility for every connection a named line in the contracts, and fund the review time so the engineer can actually check rather than stamp to meet a deadline.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is assuming a change is clerical because it looks small. The control is a written submittal procedure in which the fabricator must cloud and list every departure from the contract drawings, and the engineer must sign a recalculation for any departure that touches a load path.

The beginner's mistake

Believing that because several parties stamped a drawing, the design was checked several times. Several stamps on a change nobody recalculated is no check at all.

Callback

In Week 2, Kema taught inversion: ask what would have to be true for the plan to fail. Applied to a shop drawing, the question is not whether the detail looks right but how this change could move load somewhere it was never designed to go. That single inverted question would have found the doubled load.

Recap

A late, convenient change from one continuous rod to two rods doubled the load on an already weak connection, the shop drawing review did not recalculate it, and 114 people died. The lesson is ownership: every change to a load path needs a named engineer and a calculation. Rule 114 makes that a habit.

Next: Priya on The Money: what prefabrication and off-site steel really do to cost, carry and the lender's draw.
checklist: Every shop drawing departure from the contract design is clouded and listed by the fabricator.
Any change that alters how load is shared between members gets a signed recalculation.
One named engineer owns connection design, in writing.
A failure during construction triggers a review of every similar load path, not just the one that failed.
I never treat several stamps as several checks.
The owner's decision log records who approved each structural change and on what basis.
Submittal review time is resourced so the engineer can check, not just stamp.
head: Field checklist
speak: On 17 July 1981 two suspended walkways at the Hyatt Regency in Kansas City fell during a crowded event and 114 people died. The original design hung both walkways from one continuous rod. On the shop drawings it became two rods, which is easier to build. That small change meant the upper walkway's connection now carried both walkways, roughly doubling the load on a detail that was already weaker than code required. The drawings were reviewed and approved without a recalculation. Once the steel was made and covered, the defect was hidden. The root cause was a gap in responsibility: everyone could believe someone else had checked. The engineers lost their licences, and the case is taught as the reason the engineer of record owns structural changes that arrive through shop drawings. My rule: no change to a load path is approved without a named engineer and a calculation.
terms: Hanger rod — a steel rod that suspends a floor or walkway from structure above, carrying its load in tension.
Box beam — a hollow beam formed from plates or channels, here the walkway beam through which the rods passed.
Engineer of record — the licensed engineer responsible for the structural design shown on the permit drawings.

hostile.q: This change saved the fabricator two weeks and the engineer approved it. Why should the owner pay for an extra recalculation?
hostile.a: Because an approval without a recalculation is a signature, not a check. The change alters how load is shared between two members, and that is exactly the kind of change that has killed people. A recalculation costs a few days of an engineer's time. I will pay for that and pursue the two weeks elsewhere in the sequence.

rule: Rule 114: No change to a load path is fabricated until a named engineer has recalculated it and signed the result; a stamp without a calculation is not a check.

title: What Prefabrication and Off-Site Steel Really Cost
summary: Prefabrication and fast steel are bought for time and certainty, not a lower unit price. Price a critical-path week as interest, general conditions and forgone NOI, then compare it with the premium. Treat off-site deposits and stored materials as credit exposure that needs title, insurance and security.
body:
Steel and prefabrication do not usually make a building cheaper per piece; they make it faster and more certain. The money question is whether the weeks saved and the risk removed are worth more than the premium and the cash you must put at risk off site.

Recall

Q. In a pre-pour meeting, what three things must be confirmed before concrete is ordered?

A. That embedded items, reinforcement and cover have been inspected and signed off, that the weather and curing plan is ready, and that the pump, crew and testing agency are booked. A pour that starts before sign-off cannot be undone.

Q. How does a higher-strength concrete mix affect cost beyond the price per cubic metre?

A. It can raise cement content, heat of hydration and curing demands, and it may need more testing and tighter supply control. The total cost includes the controls, not just the delivered price.

Q. Why does elevator count and speed matter to a pro forma?

A. Elevators drive waiting time, tenant satisfaction, core area and a large long-lead cost. Too few hurt revenue; too many waste rentable area and capital.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a contractor will often offer you prefabrication, or a faster steel frame, at a premium. A developer who only compares the line items will refuse it. A developer who prices time and risk will sometimes accept it, and sometimes refuse it for better reasons. Today Priya teaches you to put a number on both sides.

What a week is worth

In plain English: every week the building is not finished costs you interest, overheads and lost rent, whether or not anyone is working.

The professional framing is the cost of carry: the time-dependent costs of a project, chiefly construction interest, general conditions such as site supervision and temporary facilities, insurance, and the net operating income (NOI) you forgo by opening later. NOI is rent and other income less operating expenses, before debt service. A week saved on the critical path removes a week of carry. A week saved on an activity with float removes nothing.

A worked example, with hypothetical round numbers. A 40,000,000 dollar project is drawing a construction loan with an average outstanding balance near the end of 25,000,000 dollars at 8 percent a year. Interest is about 2,000,000 dollars a year, or roughly 38,000 dollars a week. General conditions run 30,000 dollars a week. Stabilised NOI will be 2,600,000 dollars a year, so each week of later opening forgoes about 50,000 dollars. Together, one critical-path week is worth roughly 118,000 dollars. If prefabricated bathroom pods save 8 critical-path weeks, the time is worth about 944,000 dollars before any risk adjustment.

Say that out loud now.

The premium, and what it buys besides time

In plain English: factory work usually costs more to make but less to fix, and it moves labour off a crowded site.

Prefabrication premiums come from factory overhead, transport, cranes, design coordination done early, and the fabricator's profit and risk. Against that sit fewer trades in the building, less rework, better quality control, less weather exposure and fewer site injuries. Some of those benefits are hard to price, and an honest analysis names them rather than inventing a figure.

Continue the example. The pods carry a premium of 600,000 dollars over site-built bathrooms. Time alone is worth 944,000 dollars, so the decision looks clear. Now apply realism. Will the pods really save 8 critical-path weeks, or 8 weeks of a bathroom trade that was never critical? If the schedule shows the critical path runs through the facade, not the bathrooms, the pods may save only 2 weeks: 236,000 dollars against a 600,000 dollar premium. The same product is a good buy on one project and a poor one on another. The schedule decides, not the brochure.

Paying for things you cannot see

In plain English: a fabricator wants money before your pieces are on site, and if it fails while holding your money and your steel, you can lose both.

A new term: stored materials. These are materials paid for but not yet incorporated into the building, either on site or off site in a fabricator's yard or a bonded warehouse. Lenders and owners often pay for off-site stored materials only on conditions such as a bill of sale transferring title, insurance naming the owner, the goods being segregated and marked, and an inspection by the lender's monitor. These are commercial terms, not statutes; your loan and contract decide which apply.

A second worked example, hypothetical. The steel contract is 5,000,000 dollars. The fabricator asks for a 15 percent deposit, 750,000 dollars, to buy mill steel, then monthly payment for fabricated pieces held in its yard. By month three you have paid 2,250,000 dollars and nothing is erected. Your lender will fund only the portion supported by title documents and insurance, say 1,500,000 dollars, so the other 750,000 dollars, the deposit, is your equity at risk. If the fabricator becomes insolvent, the pieces it has marked and transferred to you are easier to recover; an unsecured deposit may join the queue of creditors. A deposit protected by an advance payment bond or a letter of credit, which is a bank's promise to pay if conditions are met, costs a fee but changes that outcome. Professional sign-off required: a construction lawyer on title and security for off-site goods.

Warrick's Wealth Ledger

On your personal balance sheet, a deposit to a supplier is not an asset you can count at face value. It is a claim on another company's solvency. If your equity in a project includes large unprotected deposits, mark it down in your own head until the goods are delivered, and remember that any guarantee you have signed makes a supplier failure a household event.

Mill price escalation

In plain English: a fabricator may refuse to fix the price of steel it has not yet bought, and ask you to carry the market risk.

An escalation clause adjusts the contract price if the cost of mill steel moves beyond a set band between bid and purchase, often tied to a published price index. It is commercial practice, not a standard, and every term is negotiable: the index, the band, the cap, and the date the price locks, usually the date the mill order is placed. A worked example, hypothetical. The frame has 600 tonnes. The clause allows adjustment for movement above 5 percent from a base of 1,500 dollars a tonne. The mill price rises 25 percent, to 1,875 dollars. The adjustable movement is 20 percent above the band, 300 dollars a tonne, so the increase is 600 times 300, which is 180,000 dollars. The cheapest protection is often to place the mill order early, which locks the price and removes the clause's reach. That links straight back to procurement dates: a late mill order is a schedule risk and a price risk at once.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is paying large deposits and stored-material invoices to a fabricator whose finances you have not checked, without title transfer or security. The control is a payment rule: no off-site payment without a bill of sale, insurance naming the owner, marked and segregated goods, an inspection, and, for deposits, an advance payment bond or letter of credit.

The beginner's mistake

Valuing time saved on any activity instead of time saved on the critical path. Only critical-path time removes carry.

Callback

In Week 40, Priya taught the in-balance test: undisbursed loan plus undisbursed equity must cover the cost to complete. Off-site stored materials the lender will not fund do not reduce cost to complete in the lender's eyes, so a big deposit can push the loan out of balance even while money is being spent exactly as planned.

Recap

Price a critical-path week as interest, general conditions and forgone NOI. Compare that against the prefabrication premium only for weeks that are truly critical. Treat off-site payments as credit exposure and protect them with title, insurance, inspection and security.

Next: Ivo on The Rules: the standards, inspections and safety rules that govern steel and factory-built work.
checklist: I can state what one critical-path week costs this project in interest, general conditions and forgone NOI.
I check the schedule to confirm a prefabricated element is on the critical path before valuing time saved.
I compare any prefabrication premium against realistic, not brochure, weeks saved.
No off-site payment is made without a bill of sale, insurance naming the owner, segregated goods and an inspection.
Large deposits are protected by an advance payment bond or letter of credit.
I have checked the fabricator's financial strength before paying a deposit.
I know which stored materials my lender will fund and which are my equity at risk.
head: Field checklist
speak: Prefabrication and fast steel rarely cost less per piece. They buy time and certainty. So I price a critical-path week: construction interest, general conditions like supervision, and the net operating income I lose by opening later. On a hypothetical project that is about 118,000 dollars a week. Then I check the schedule. If the prefabricated element is not on the critical path, the weeks saved are worth nothing, and a 600,000 dollar premium is wasted. Off-site work brings a second cost: money paid before I can see the goods. Deposits and stored-material payments are really loans to the fabricator. My lender may refuse to fund them without title and insurance, which makes them my equity at risk. So I insist on a bill of sale, insurance naming me, goods marked and segregated, an inspection, and an advance payment bond or letter of credit for any deposit. A lawyer signs off on the title and security.
terms: Cost of carry — the time-dependent costs of a project, such as interest, general conditions and forgone income, incurred for every week it runs.
Stored materials — materials paid for but not yet built into the work, held on site or off site.
Letter of credit — a bank's undertaking to pay a named beneficiary when stated conditions are met.

hostile.q: You want me to fund 2,250,000 dollars of steel sitting in a yard I have never seen. Why is that any different from unsecured lending to your fabricator?
hostile.a: It is not different unless we make it so, and I agree you should not fund it on trust. I will give you a bill of sale for each released sequence, insurance naming the owner and you as loss payee, goods marked and segregated in the yard, and an inspection by your monitor before each draw. The 750,000 dollar deposit is my equity, and it is backed by an advance payment bond. Fund only what those documents support.

title: The Standards Stack for Steel and Factory-Built Work
summary: The building code ties together the standards for steel design, fabrication, welding, bolting and erection safety. Shop work needs special inspection unless the fabricator is approved under a recognised program. Ownership of goods held off site depends on the contract's vesting clause and the law of sale of goods.
body:
Steel and factory-built work are governed by a stack of standards for design, fabrication, welding, bolting, erection safety and inspection. You do not need to read them all; you need to know which one answers which question, and who is responsible for proving compliance.

Recall

Q. What is cost of carry?

A. The time-dependent costs of a project, such as interest, general conditions and forgone income, paid for every week the work runs. Only critical-path time saved removes it.

Q. What does a cylinder test under ASTM C39 measure?

A. The compressive strength of a concrete cylinder made and cured under a standard method, usually tested at set ages to confirm the specified strength. Verify the current edition before you rely on details.

Q. What is a design flood elevation used for?

A. It sets the level to which a building, its lowest floor and its critical equipment must be raised or protected against the design flood, often with an added freeboard.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, when a steel connection or a factory-built module is questioned, the argument always comes down to one of three things: what standard applied, who was responsible under it, and what record proves it was met. Ivo teaches the map so you can find the right page fast and know which licensed professional to call.

The standards stack

In plain English: one set of rules for how steel is designed, another for how it is made, another for how it is welded and bolted, another for how it is put up safely, and the building code ties them together.

The professional framing runs like this. The International Building Code (IBC), as adopted by your jurisdiction, is the legal backbone, and it references other standards by edition. For structural steel, design follows AISC 360, the Specification for Structural Steel Buildings, with AISC 341 added where seismic design requires it. Responsibility between owner, designer, fabricator and erector is described in AISC 303, the Code of Standard Practice, which many contracts adopt by reference. Welding follows AWS D1.1, the Structural Welding Code for steel, which covers welding procedures, welder qualification and inspection. High-strength bolted joints follow the specification of the Research Council on Structural Connections, which sets how bolts are tightened and checked. Materials are specified by ASTM standards, for example for wide-flange shapes, plates and bolts. Verify every edition and which ones your jurisdiction has adopted against the current adopted edition.

A worked example of using the map. An inspector finds that some bolts on a moment connection were tightened only snug, not pretensioned. Which standard answers the question? The drawings and specification say what type of joint was required. The bolting specification says how a pretensioned joint is installed and verified. The IBC and its special inspection provisions say who must verify it. Three documents, three questions, one answer: the joint does not comply until it is pretensioned and verified by the method the specification allows.

Say that out loud now.

Erection safety: OSHA 1926 Subpart R

In plain English: federal rules say how steel may be put up without killing the people putting it up.

In the United States, steel erection safety falls under OSHA 1926 Subpart R. Its topics include written notification that concrete footings and anchor bolts are ready before erection starts, column anchorage and stability during erection, beam and column connection practice, controlled decking zones and fall protection for connectors. Verify the current text before you rely on it. As owner, you are not the erector, but under the multi-employer doctrine taught in Week 53 an owner who controls the site can attract obligations. The practical step is to require the erector's written site-specific erection plan and to make sure the controlling contractor enforces it.

Factory-built work: who inspects what you cannot walk

In plain English: work done in a factory still has to be inspected, but the inspector may not be able to visit, so the rules lean on approved fabricators and third-party programs.

A new term: approved fabricator. Under the IBC's special inspection provisions, work done in a fabricator's shop is generally subject to special inspection unless the fabricator is approved, for example through a recognised certification program, in which case the fabricator files a certificate of compliance at completion [unverified — confirm independently]. AISC runs a fabricator and erector certification program, and building officials often accept certified fabricators in place of shop inspections. Verify against the current adopted edition.

Volumetric modules and other factory-built buildings may also fall under state or provincial modular programs, in which a third-party agency inspects in the plant and attaches a label, and the local building official then inspects only the site work and the connections between modules. Programs vary widely by state; do not assume, ask the building official at pre-application.

A second worked example. A developer buys structural steel from an uncertified shop to save money. The building official requires shop special inspection, so the owner must now pay an inspection agency to travel to the shop for each critical weld and bolted assembly. Over 8 months, at a hypothetical 12,000 dollars a month in travel and inspection time, the saving of 50,000 dollars on the steel price becomes a loss of 46,000 dollars, plus schedule risk whenever the inspector is not available.

Title to off-site work: the contract governs

Ownership of goods still in a fabricator's yard is usually decided by the contract and by the law of sale of goods; in most American states that is Article 2 of the Uniform Commercial Code, as enacted. A well-drafted steel subcontract includes a vesting clause, which states when title passes to the owner, such as on payment or on marking and segregation, and requires the goods to be insured and identified. Verify the enacted version in your state before you rely on it. Professional sign-off required: a construction lawyer on vesting and on how a vesting clause behaves if the fabricator becomes insolvent.

The records the rules expect

In plain English: compliance is proved by paper, and the paper has to exist before the steel is buried.

For structural steel, the usual record set includes certified mill test reports tracing each heat of steel to its chemistry and strength, welding procedure specifications and welder qualification records under AWS D1.1, bolt and nut lot certificates, inspection reports from the special inspector, and the fabricator's certificate of compliance where it is approved. Fireproofing adds thickness and density test records. Ask for the list in the specification, ask who keeps each record, and make delivery of the record set a condition of final payment. A building official or a buyer's engineer years later will ask for exactly these documents, and they are almost impossible to recreate once the frame is enclosed.

Two Systems is next week

This is an even week, so there is no Canada and Guyana comparison today. One general point still travels: wherever you build, ask early which steel and welding standards the authority will accept, and whether it will accept shop inspection done by an agency in another country. An authority that does not recognise a foreign fabricator's certification can force inspection on every shipment, and that answer belongs in the procurement plan, not in a surprise at the port.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is assuming the fabricator's own quality control satisfies the building official. The control is to ask the official, before buying, whether the fabricator is approved for this work and what shop inspection will otherwise be required, and to price the answer.

The beginner's mistake

Naming standards in a specification without naming editions, then discovering mid-project that the fabricator, the inspector and the official are reading different years.

Callback

In Week 100, Ivo taught that the code basis, meaning occupancy and construction type, is set first and everything follows from it. Steel is the same: construction type decides the fireproofing the steel needs, which Week 102 covered with Magnus, and that fireproofing is a submittal, an inspection and a cost that must appear in the steel package.

Recap

The IBC binds the stack; AISC 360 and 341 govern design, AISC 303 shares responsibility, AWS D1.1 governs welding, the bolting specification governs bolts, and OSHA 1926 Subpart R governs erection safety. Shop work needs special inspection unless the fabricator is approved. Title to off-site goods is a contract and sale-of-goods question.

Next: Quincy on The Numbers: reverse engineering a finished steel frame from its cost and erection time.
checklist: My specification names each standard and its edition.
I have asked the building official whether my fabricator is approved for shop work.
I have priced shop special inspection if the fabricator is not approved.
The erector has a written site-specific erection plan that meets OSHA 1926 Subpart R.
Footing and anchor bolt readiness is notified in writing before erection starts.
The steel subcontract has a vesting clause and insurance requirement for off-site goods.
A construction lawyer has reviewed vesting and insolvency protection.
head: Field checklist
speak: Steel is governed by a stack of standards, and each one answers a different question. The building code, as adopted locally, is the legal backbone. AISC 360 governs how steel is designed, with AISC 341 for seismic work. AISC 303, the Code of Standard Practice, shares responsibility between owner, designer, fabricator and erector. AWS D1.1 covers welding, and the Research Council on Structural Connections covers high-strength bolts. Erection safety falls under OSHA 1926 Subpart R. Work done in a shop generally needs special inspection unless the fabricator is approved, so before I buy I ask the building official whether my fabricator qualifies, because travelling inspectors can wipe out a price saving. Factory-built modules may fall under a state program with plant inspection and labels. And who owns steel still in the yard depends on the contract's vesting clause and sale-of-goods law, so a construction lawyer reviews it.
terms: Approved fabricator — a fabricator recognised by the building official, often through a certification program, whose shop work may be accepted without separate special inspection.
Vesting clause — a contract term stating when title to goods or work passes to the owner.
Special inspection — inspection required by the building code for critical work, performed by a qualified inspector working for the owner rather than the contractor.

hostile.q: The building official wants special inspection at your fabricator's shop two states away. Why didn't you plan for that?
hostile.a: I should have asked before award, and the lesson is noted in our decision log. Now the fix is either to confirm whether the fabricator can be accepted through its certification, or to contract an inspection agency near the shop. I will have the cost and a schedule of critical inspections to you by Friday, and I will not let fabrication run ahead of the inspections.

title: Reverse Engineering a Finished Steel Frame
summary: Starting from a finished frame's cost and erection time, work backward to tonnage, the installed rate per tonne and its parts, picks per day for the crane, and the dates detailing and mill orders had to start. The same method gives the break-even premium for prefabrication.
body:
You can learn how a steel frame was planned by starting from two finished facts, its cost and its erection time, and working backward to the tonnage, the rate per tonne, the picks per day and the date the mill order had to be placed.

Recall

Q. What is a vesting clause?

A. A contract term stating when title to goods or work passes to the owner, for example on payment or on marking and segregation. It matters most if a fabricator becomes insolvent.

Q. What does a pre-pour checklist protect against?

A. Pouring concrete over reinforcement, embeds or formwork that have not been inspected and accepted. Once concrete is placed, the defect is buried.

Q. What are the four control layers of a building envelope?

A. Water, air, vapour and thermal control. Each must be continuous, and the transitions between them are where envelopes fail.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a contractor's steel price and schedule arrive as two numbers. If you can reverse engineer them, you can tell in an hour whether they hang together, whether the crane plan is real, and whether the procurement dates are already too late. This is an even week, so Quincy starts from the finished outcome and works backward.

The finished outcome

A hypothetical steel-framed building is complete. The frame cost 3,000,000 dollars. It was erected in 15 working weeks with one tower crane. The gross floor area is 20,000 square metres. Every number below is hypothetical and round.

Step 1: back out the tonnage

Steel frames are commonly benchmarked by weight per unit of floor area. Suppose the engineer's take-off showed 30 kilograms of structural steel per square metre, which is a plausible order for a regular mid-rise frame but varies widely with spans, loads and lateral system. Then the frame weighs 20,000 square metres times 30 kilograms, which is 600,000 kilograms, or 600 tonnes.

Step 2: back out the rate per tonne and split it

3,000,000 dollars divided by 600 tonnes is 5,000 dollars per tonne, installed. A quantity surveyor splits that installed rate into its parts. Suppose the split was: mill steel 1,500 dollars per tonne, fabrication including connections and shop labour 1,800, shop drawings and connection engineering 300, delivery 200, erection including crane and crew 1,000, and painting or primer 200. Add them: 1,500 plus 1,800 plus 300 plus 200 plus 1,000 plus 200 is 5,000 dollars per tonne. The useful insight is that the mill steel, the part most exposed to market prices, is under a third of the cost. A 20 percent rise in mill price moves the installed rate by only 300 dollars per tonne, 6 percent of the total.

Say that out loud now.

Step 3: back out the crane picks per day

Suppose the frame has 2,400 pieces. Fifteen weeks of five working days is 75 days. 2,400 pieces divided by 75 days is 32 pieces a day. If the crane works a 10-hour day, that is 3.2 picks an hour, or one pick about every 19 minutes, including rigging, lifting, landing and the connector making the first bolts safe. That is achievable for routine beams but tight if many pieces are heavy or awkward, and it leaves no room for wind days. If the site loses 10 days to weather, the remaining 65 days need about 37 pieces a day, or one every 16 minutes. This single calculation tells you whether the 15-week claim was realistic or optimistic, and whether a second crane or a mobile crane for heavy picks was in the plan.

Step 4: back out the procurement dates

Now work backward from the first erection day, call it day zero. Suppose the fabricator needs 6 weeks from approved drawings to first delivery, the engineer's review takes 2 weeks, detailing the first sequence takes 6 weeks, and the mill needs 8 weeks to roll and deliver the steel. Shop drawing work and the mill order can run in parallel once the design is frozen. So the first approved drawings are needed 6 weeks before day zero, first submission 8 weeks before, detailing must start 14 weeks before, and the mill order must be placed by about 14 weeks before as well, so the steel arrives in the shop at week 6 before day zero, just as fabrication starts. Allow one resubmittal cycle of 2 weeks, and detailing must start 16 weeks before erection. If the contract was signed 12 weeks before the planned erection date, the plan was late on the day it was signed.

A second worked example: the prefabrication break-even premium

Reverse the money question from Day 3. You are told that prefabricated stair and core modules saved 6 critical-path weeks, and that the project's cost of carry was 100,000 dollars a week. The most the owner should have paid as a premium, before risk, is 6 times 100,000 dollars, which is 600,000 dollars. If the owner also believed the modules removed a realistic risk of a further 2 weeks of delay with a probability of one in four, the expected value of that risk reduction is 2 weeks times 100,000 dollars times 0.25, which is 50,000 dollars. So the break-even premium was about 650,000 dollars. Any premium above that was paid for something else, such as quality or safety, and should have been justified in those terms.

A third check: does the cost per square metre agree?

3,000,000 dollars over 20,000 square metres is 150 dollars per square metre for the frame. Quincy compares that with the cost plan from design. If the cost plan said 120 dollars per square metre, the extra 30 dollars per square metre, 600,000 dollars in total, must be explained: heavier steel than assumed, a costlier connection type, or a tighter erection schedule paid for in crane time.

Step 5: what the reverse engineering tells you to ask

The point of working backward is the questions it produces. From this frame, Quincy would ask the contractor five things. What weight per square metre did the engineer assume, and why does it differ from similar frames? Which line of the installed rate carries the most risk, and is it fixed or subject to escalation? What is the piece count, the crane plan and the weather allowance behind the erection duration? When must detailing start and when must the mill order be placed to meet the first erection day, and are those dates already in the schedule? And which prefabricated elements sit on the critical path, so that their premium can be tested against the cost of carry? Five questions, each answerable in a page. A contractor who cannot answer them has not planned the frame; a contractor who answers them quickly has, and you can trust the number more.

Why reverse engineering beats checking line items

A line-by-line check asks whether each number looks reasonable on its own. Reverse engineering asks whether the numbers agree with each other. A low rate per tonne, a short erection duration and a late contract date can each look plausible alone, while together they describe a frame nobody can build on time. The method finds contradictions, and contradictions are where the money is lost.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is accepting an erection duration without checking picks per day against the number of pieces. The control is to ask the erector for its piece count, crane plan and weather allowance, and to run Step 3 yourself before signing.

The beginner's mistake

Treating the mill steel price as the whole cost of steel. Fabrication, engineering and erection usually make up most of the installed rate.

Callback

In Week 50, Petra taught that float belongs to someone and that the critical path decides the finish. Step 4 is the same discipline applied to procurement: the mill order and the shop drawings are activities with their own durations, and if they start late they consume the float of the whole job before a single beam is lifted.

Recap

From cost and duration, back out tonnage, rate per tonne and its split, picks per day and procurement dates. Mill steel is a minority of installed cost. Picks per day reveals whether the schedule is real. Detailing and mill orders must start well before the contract many owners sign too late.

Next: Bram on The Room: the meeting where the fabricator asks to change connections and increase its deposit.
checklist: I ask for the steel weight per square metre and compare it with similar frames.
I split the installed rate per tonne into mill, fabrication, engineering, delivery, erection and coating.
I check picks per day against the piece count and the crane plan.
I add a weather allowance before accepting an erection duration.
I schedule detailing and the mill order backward from the first erection day.
I price the break-even premium for any prefabrication offer.
I reconcile the frame cost per square metre with the design cost plan.
head: Field checklist
speak: I can test any steel price and schedule by working backward. Start with cost and duration: a hypothetical 3,000,000 dollar frame erected in 15 weeks on 20,000 square metres. At 30 kilograms per square metre, that is 600 tonnes, so 5,000 dollars per tonne installed. Split it, and mill steel is under a third; fabrication, engineering and erection are the rest, so a jump in mill price moves the total less than people fear. Then picks per day: 2,400 pieces over 75 days is 32 a day, about one every 19 minutes, with nothing left for wind. That tells me whether the duration is real. Then procurement: work backward from the first erection day through fabrication, review, detailing and the mill order, and I find detailing must start about four months before steel is lifted. Finally the prefabrication break-even: weeks saved times the weekly cost of carry, plus the expected value of risk removed.
terms: Installed rate — the total cost per unit, here per tonne, including material, fabrication, engineering, delivery and erection.
Pick — one crane lift, from rigging the load to releasing it once it is safely connected.
Break-even premium — the highest extra price worth paying for an option, equal to the value of the time and risk it removes.

hostile.q: Your contractor promises 15 weeks for steel erection with one crane. Why should I believe it?
hostile.a: I tested it. The frame has about 2,400 pieces, which is 32 picks a day over 75 working days, roughly one every 19 minutes with no weather allowance. That is tight. I have asked the erector for its crane plan, its heavy-pick strategy and its weather days, and I am carrying 2 extra weeks in my own schedule until it shows me the plan holds.

title: When the Fabricator Wants a New Connection and a Bigger Deposit
summary: A late fabricator bundles a connection change with a deposit increase and the contractor wants a yes today. Split the two, send the connection to the engineer of record with calculations, treat the deposit as a credit question secured by goods or a bond, and give dated answers.
body:
The hardest steel meeting is not about price. It is the one where the fabricator, behind schedule, asks to change connection details and raise its deposit in the same breath, and the contractor wants you to agree before you leave the room.

Recall

Q. What is the installed rate per tonne made of?

A. Mill steel, fabrication, shop drawings and connection engineering, delivery, erection and coating. Mill steel is usually a minority of the total.

Q. What does OSHA 1926 Subpart R cover?

A. Steel erection safety, including notification that footings and anchor bolts are ready, column stability, connecting practice, decking and fall protection. Verify the current text.

Q. What is a time impact analysis used for?

A. To show how a specific delay event changes the critical path and the completion date, by inserting the event into the schedule and measuring the result.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, a developer is tested most when two requests are bundled so that saying yes to the reasonable one carries the dangerous one with it. Bram takes you through the scene, because the technical answer is simple and the human one is not.

The scene

Week 18 of a hypothetical job. Present: you, your owner's representative, the general contractor's project manager, and the steel fabricator's owner on a video call. The fabricator is three weeks late releasing the second sequence. It proposes two things. First, to change 120 beam-to-column shear connections from a bolted plate to a welded detail its shop prefers, which it says will recover two weeks. Second, to raise its deposit by 300,000 dollars because mill prices have moved. The contractor says, with real warmth, that you are all on the same side and it would like a yes today so the shop can start Monday.

The question behind the question

The question behind the connection change is whether anyone has recalculated the load path; Rule 114 says no change is fabricated until a named engineer has. The question behind the deposit is whether the fabricator is short of cash. A shop that needs more money up front while running late may be in financial trouble, and an extra deposit is an unsecured loan to a company that may fail. Bundling the two requests also tells you something: the deposit is easier to win if it rides on the schedule recovery everyone wants.

The lines to say

"I want the two weeks back, and I want to understand both requests properly, so let me take them one at a time."

"On the connections: please send the proposed detail with the fabricator engineer's calculations to the engineer of record today. I will ask for a review in three working days, and the shop can start on pieces that are unaffected."

"On the deposit: show me the mill quotes and your current order book, and tell me how the deposit would be secured. I will consider it against an advance payment bond or a bill of sale for marked material."

"What else is causing the three-week slip, apart from these two items?"

Say that out loud now.

The lines never to say

"If the engineer is fine with it, so am I." This hands your decision to a review that has not happened.

"We will sort the paperwork later." Later is when the steel is erected and the deposit is spent.

"I trust you." Trust is not a control, and the fabricator will remember you offered it.

When to stay silent

After you ask what else is causing the slip, stop talking. The pause is uncomfortable, and the fabricator will fill it. That answer, a shop loading problem, a lost welder, a late mill delivery, is the real information in the meeting. If you fill the silence yourself, you will never hear it.

Holding your state

The contractor's warmth is pressure. Notice it, name it to yourself, and slow your speech. You are allowed to say: "I will give you an answer on each item by Thursday." Then give it on Thursday. A firm date is more reassuring to everyone than a rushed yes, and it is what experienced owners do.

A worked example of the follow-up

By Thursday, hypothetical results arrive. The engineer accepts 100 of the 120 welded connections and rejects 20 where the column web is too thin for the new detail. The fabricator's order book shows heavy workload and a supplier dispute. You decide: approve the 100 connections, keep the bolted detail for the 20, and agree to 150,000 dollars of the 300,000 dollar deposit increase, paid only against a bill of sale for marked mill steel in the yard, insured in your name, inspected by the lender's monitor. The schedule recovers about a week and a half. Your exposure to the fabricator's balance sheet rises by nothing that is not backed by goods you own.

A second check on the numbers: at a hypothetical cost of carry of 100,000 dollars a critical-path week, the week and a half recovered is worth 150,000 dollars. You have paid for that recovery with a three-day review, not with an unsecured advance, and you have protected the 20 connections that could have failed.

Monthly thread: working with advisers

This meeting worked because you had an engineer of record who could review fast, an owner's representative who knew the shop, and a lawyer who had drafted a vesting clause. Advisers are most useful when they are engaged before the crisis, with authority and fees agreed, so that a three-day review is a phone call rather than a negotiation.

Ask yourself a question: which adviser on your future team do you not yet have a working relationship with, and what would it cost you to find out in the middle of a meeting like this one?

Reading the fabricator's financial signals

Deposit requests are rarely the only sign. Practitioners watch for a cluster: a request to be paid earlier or more often, missed release dates without a clear technical cause, supplier disputes, key staff leaving, reluctance to show the order book, and a sudden willingness to accept terms the shop resisted a month ago. One signal proves little. Three together justify asking for current financial information, tightening payment to goods you own, and quietly identifying a second shop that could take over a sequence. None of this needs to be said aloud in the meeting. It needs to be in your notes, in your decision log, and in a call to your lawyer about what the contract allows you to do if the shop fails.

What the contractor needs from you

The contractor's project manager is not your opponent in this meeting. It is under pressure from its own schedule and its own subcontractor, and it wants a decision it can act on. Give it one: a dated review for the connections, a clear list of what you need for the deposit, and permission to keep the shop working on unaffected pieces. A contractor that leaves with three concrete actions and a Thursday date usually stops pushing for a yes in the room, because it can now report progress upward. The warmth it showed at the start was a request for certainty. You can give certainty about the process without giving away the decision.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk is agreeing to a bundled request because one half is attractive. The control is to split every bundled request into its parts and decide each on its own evidence and its own date.

The beginner's mistake

Answering in the room to show decisiveness. Decisiveness is giving a firm date and keeping it.

Callback

In Week 6, Kema taught the line "I'll confirm by Friday" as a way to hold a hostile question without bluffing. Here it becomes a control: a dated commitment turns pressure for an immediate yes into a short, defined review, and the date is kept.

Recap

Split bundled requests. Send connection changes to the engineer of record with calculations. Treat a deposit increase from a late fabricator as a credit question and secure it with goods or a bond. Ask what else is causing the slip, then stay silent. Give dated answers and keep them.

Next: Kema on Quiz and Recap: the week's six questions, a Red Pen drill and the boardroom drill.
checklist: I split every bundled request into its parts.
Connection changes go to the engineer of record with calculations before fabrication.
Unaffected pieces keep moving while a change is reviewed.
I treat a deposit increase from a late fabricator as a credit question.
Any extra deposit is secured by marked goods, insurance and inspection, or by a bond.
I ask what else is causing the slip and then stay silent.
I give a firm answer date and keep it.
head: Field checklist
speak: The fabricator is three weeks late. It wants to change 120 connections to recover two weeks and to raise its deposit by 300,000 dollars, and the contractor wants a yes today. I split the two. The connection change goes to the engineer of record with the fabricator engineer's calculations, with a three-day review, while unaffected pieces keep moving, because no change to a load path is built until someone has recalculated it. The deposit is a credit question: a late shop asking for more cash up front may be in trouble, so I want mill quotes, its order book and security, either a bill of sale for marked material or a bond. Then I ask what else is causing the slip, and I stay silent until they answer. I give a firm date for each decision and keep it. In the example, I approved most of the connections, kept the old detail where the column was too thin, and paid half the deposit against goods I own.
terms: Bundled request — two or more asks presented together so that agreeing to one carries the others.
Advance payment bond — a surety's or bank's undertaking to repay an advance if the supplier fails to perform.
Owner's representative — a person or firm acting for the owner to manage the project and its contractors day to day.

hostile.q: We are losing a day for every day you take to decide. Why won't you just approve both today?
hostile.a: Because I want the two weeks back, not a failed connection or an unsecured loan. The connection change is with the engineer today and I have asked for three working days; the shop can keep working on unaffected pieces. On the deposit I need the mill quotes and the security proposal. You will have my decision on both by Thursday.

role: Chief of staff and learning coach
title: Week 114 Review: Steel, Connections and Off-Site Work
summary: Six questions test the week: connections and the load path, delegated design, the Hyatt Regency collapse, valuing prefabrication time, shop inspection and protecting off-site payments. A Red Pen drill finds six defects in a steel subcontract clause, and the boardroom drill explains the week in two minutes.
body:
This week came down to one sentence: steel is designed twice, the shop drawings and connections decide whether the second design is safe, and every dollar or change that moves off site needs an owner, a calculation and a record.

Recall

Q. What is a bundled request, and how do you handle one?

A. Two or more asks presented together so that agreeing to one carries the others. Split them and decide each on its own evidence and date.

Q. What is the difference between an engineer's review stamp and a guarantee?

A. A review stamp usually confirms general conformance with design intent. It does not normally guarantee every dimension or relieve the fabricator of its own duty.

Q. What does commissioning intent mean at the design stage?

A. A statement of how each system is meant to perform, written early so that design, installation and testing can all be checked against it.

Why this matters

Mr Shabazz, if you can answer these six questions without notes, you can sit with an engineer of record, a fabricator and a lender and follow every decision that matters about the frame. Answer each aloud before reading the answer.

The six questions

Question 1. Why are connections the heart of a steel frame's safety?

Answer: Because the load path runs through them: force changes direction and concentrates at every connection, so a strong member with a weak connection is a weak structure.

Question 2. What is delegated connection design, and what must the contract say about it?

Answer: The engineer of record gives connection forces and a licensed engineer for the fabricator designs the connections. The contract must state which method applies, who stamps the calculations and who reviews them.

Question 3. What went wrong at the Hyatt Regency in 1981?

Answer: A continuous hanger rod was changed to two rods on the shop drawings, doubling the load on an already weak connection. The change was approved without a recalculation, and the walkways collapsed, killing 114 people.

Question 4. How do you value time saved by prefabrication?

Answer: Multiply critical-path weeks saved by the weekly cost of carry, meaning interest, general conditions and forgone NOI, and add the expected value of any risk removed. Weeks not on the critical path are worth nothing.

Question 5. When is shop work accepted without separate special inspection?

Answer: Generally when the fabricator is approved by the building official, often through a recognised certification program. Confirm with the official before award.

Question 6. What protects you when you pay for steel still in a fabricator's yard?

Answer: A vesting clause and bill of sale transferring title, insurance naming the owner, goods marked and segregated, an inspection, and for deposits an advance payment bond or letter of credit.

Say that out loud now.

Recap of the week

Bram framed steel as designed twice, with the load path running through connections and a half-built frame needing its own stability plan. Ford took the Hyatt Regency walkways through seven steps, giving Rule 114. Priya priced a critical-path week and treated off-site payments as credit exposure. Ivo mapped the standards stack and the rules for shop inspection and title. Quincy reverse engineered a finished frame from cost and duration. Bram ran the meeting where a late fabricator bundled a connection change with a deposit.

Red Pen

Read this hypothetical steel subcontract clause and find the defects before reading on.

Connections. The Fabricator shall design all connections to suit its shop practice. Shop drawings shall be deemed approved if the Engineer does not respond within 5 days. Minor changes to connection details may be made without resubmittal. The Owner shall pay 25 percent of the Subcontract Sum on signing and monthly for steel fabricated, wherever located. Title passes on delivery to site. The Erector shall provide temporary bracing as it sees fit.

The defects. First, connection design to suit shop practice gives no design forces, no stamp and no review by the engineer of record. Second, deemed approval after 5 days turns silence into acceptance and ignores the real review period. Third, minor changes without resubmittal is exactly the Hyatt Regency gap; minor is undefined and a change to the load path can look minor. Fourth, a 25 percent deposit on signing is unsecured, with no bond or letter of credit. Fifth, paying for steel wherever located while title passes only on delivery means you pay for goods you do not own. Sixth, temporary bracing as it sees fit gives no written erection plan and no engineer.

The boardroom drill

Explain this week to a board in two minutes, then compare with the model answer.

Model answer: "Our steel frame is designed twice: once by our engineer, and again by the fabricator on shop drawings, which is what actually gets built. Safety lives in the connections, so our contract names who designs them, who stamps the calculations and how long review takes, and any change to a connection goes back to our engineer with calculations before it is made. That rule exists because of the Hyatt Regency collapse in 1981, where one unchecked connection change killed 114 people. Financially, steel and prefabrication buy time. We value only critical-path weeks, at interest, overheads and lost income, against any premium. Off-site payments are credit risk, so we pay only against title, insurance, marked goods and inspection, and deposits are bonded. The erector has a written stability plan, and we confirmed with the building official that the fabricator is approved for shop work."

Score yourself: did you open with the bottom line, name the connection rule and its reason, value only critical-path time, and protect off-site money? If not, record it again tomorrow.

The corrected clause

Here is how the same clause reads once the defects are removed, still hypothetical. The Engineer of Record shall provide connection forces; the Fabricator's licensed engineer shall design and stamp the connections, and the Engineer of Record shall review them within 10 working days. Every departure from the contract drawings shall be clouded and listed, and any change to a connection shall be resubmitted with calculations before fabrication. Deposits shall be secured by an advance payment bond. Payment for off-site steel shall be made only against a bill of sale, insurance naming the Owner, marking and segregation of the goods, and inspection, and title shall pass on payment. The Erector shall submit a written erection and temporary bracing plan prepared by a qualified engineer before steel is delivered. Notice that each correction gives a named person, a document or a date. That is the pattern of every good clause.

The hard follow-up in the boardroom

After the two-minute answer, a board member will often ask the sharp question: "If our fabricator failed tomorrow, what would we lose?" Practise the answer. "We would lose the unsecured part of any payment, which our contract keeps to zero by paying only against title, insurance and marked goods, with the deposit bonded. We would lose time while a second shop took over, which we would price at our weekly cost of carry. And we would keep every stamped shop drawing and calculation, because they belong to the project, so a new shop could start from them." A board that hears a loss stated precisely, with the controls that cap it, trusts the rest of what you say.

The biggest risk

The biggest risk this week is letting a change or a payment move off site without a named owner and a record. The control is the same in both cases: a calculation for every load-path change and a security document for every off-site dollar.

The beginner's mistake

Thinking that steel risk is mainly price risk. Most of the danger is in connections, schedule and off-site exposure, not the mill price.

Callback

In Week 83, Cole taught that an independent review is worth only what its scope allows. A shop drawing review is an independent review with a narrow scope; this week showed why you must know exactly what it covers and add a recalculation where the scope stops.

Recap

Connections carry the load path. Shop drawings are the real design. Changes need calculations. Time is valued on the critical path. Off-site money needs title and security. Rule 114: no change to a load path is fabricated until a named engineer has recalculated it.

speak: This week, steel. The frame is designed twice: by our engineer, and again by the fabricator on shop drawings, which is what gets built. Safety lives in the connections, because the load path runs through them, so the contract names who designs, stamps and reviews them, and any change goes back to the engineer with calculations first. That is Rule 114, and its reason is the Hyatt Regency collapse of 1981, where an unchecked change from one hanger rod to two doubled the load on a connection and 114 people died. A half-built frame needs a written stability plan. Financially, steel and prefabrication buy time, so I value only critical-path weeks at interest, overheads and lost income. Off-site payments are credit risk, so I pay against title, insurance, marked goods and inspection, and I bond any deposit. And I confirm with the building official, before award, whether the fabricator's shop work needs special inspection.
terms: Load path — the continuous route by which loads travel from where they are applied down to the foundations.
Deemed approval — a contract term treating silence after a set period as acceptance.
Shop practice — a fabricator's preferred methods and details, which may differ from the design.

hostile.q: Your subcontract lets the fabricator make minor connection changes without resubmittal. Who decides what is minor?
hostile.a: Nobody should, which is why that clause comes out. Any change to a connection detail goes back to the engineer of record with calculations, and the fabricator clouds and lists every departure on its submittals. Minor is exactly the word that hid the Hyatt Regency change.
